title: You Keep Calling It a Habit Because “Bondage” Sounds Too Serious.
paragraphs: You Keep Calling It a Habit Because “Bondage” Sounds Too Serious.
The most dangerous chain may be the one you keep renaming so you never have to admit that it is holding you.
You keep calling it a habit.
A habit is something you will eventually get around to changing.
A habit lets you say, “I should probably stop.”
Bondage forces a much harder question:
“Why do I keep returning to something I say I want freedom from?”
And maybe that question just made your stomach tighten.
Because you know exactly what “it” is.
Your church friends certainly don't know.
Maybe people see you worship, laugh, work, serve, post Bible verses, encourage everybody else...
but they don't see the moment when the door closes.
The secret relationship pulls you back again.
Or whatever your particular hiding place happens to be.
You told yourself it would only happen once.
And somewhere along the way, you stopped asking whether you were free and started becoming very good at explaining why what controls you isn't really controlling you.
That is why Paul's words are so unsettling.
“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be mastered by anything.”
I will not be mastered by anything.
The Greek verb is devastatingly appropriate:
It carries the idea of being brought under another's authority or mastery.
Paul's concern isn't merely, “Can I do this?”
Because perhaps the question isn't whether you can stop.
Perhaps the question is why you keep needing to prove that you can.
Then why does the thought of losing it make you uncomfortable?
Why do you keep protecting it?
Why do you become defensive when somebody questions it?
Why have you hidden how often you do it?
Why have you deleted the evidence?
Why have you promised God you would stop...
and then found yourself standing in the same place again?
This isn't written to diagnose every repeated behavior as clinical addiction. Human struggles are complex, and not every bad habit is an addiction.
But Scripture gives us no permission to make peace with something simply because we found a softer name for it.
There is a difference between struggling against something and quietly arranging your life so that you can keep surrendering to it.
And some of us have become experts at vocabulary.
We call drunkenness “taking the edge off.”
We call rage “just how I am.”
Because if we call them chains, we might finally have to admit that we need freedom.
And freedom can be frightening because freedom requires truth.
Jesus said that those who continue in His word will know the truth, and the truth will set them free.
Notice what Christ connects with freedom.
And truth sometimes begins with an embarrassingly simple sentence:
“Jesus, this has more power over me than I want anyone to know.”
Maybe you love Jesus deeply and still recognize yourself here.
Your struggle does not make the Gospel irrelevant.
It reveals how desperately you need everything the Gospel actually promises.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people can improve themselves.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners can be rescued by a Savior.
And the context surrounding 1 Corinthians 6:12 matters enormously.
Immediately before Paul's warning about being mastered, he reminds the Corinthians of what some of them once were.
Then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in the chapter:
Then Paul points to what God had done.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Paul does not confront sin by removing grace.
He confronts sin because grace has created a new identity.
“Clean yourself up sufficiently, and perhaps Jesus will receive you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds forgiveness that cannot be purchased, manufactured, performed, or deserved.
But grace does not teach us to decorate our chains.
Grace teaches us that chains no longer have the right to define us.
That is why this article isn't saying, “Try harder.”
Swore this was the last time harder.
and wondered whether Jesus finally became disgusted too.
The answer to bondage isn't simply stronger disgust toward yourself.
It is deeper surrender to Christ accompanied by honest, concrete steps into the light.
Sometimes spiritual warfare looks remarkably practical.
It looks like confessing what you have hidden.
It looks like calling a mature believer and saying, “I need help.”
It looks like refusing the environment where you repeatedly fall.
For substance dependence or another serious addiction, it may mean seeking qualified medical or professional treatment rather than trying to survive withdrawal or recovery alone.
Getting appropriate help is not evidence that prayer failed.
You can pray while making the phone call.
You can trust Jesus while entering treatment.
You can believe Scripture while sitting across from a counselor.
You can depend upon the Holy Spirit while giving trusted believers permission to ask questions you would rather avoid.
God's grace and responsible action are not enemies.
Sometimes one of the bravest prayers a Christian can pray is:
“Lord, give me enough humility to stop hiding.”
Because secrecy feeds what confession exposes.
James tells believers to confess sins to one another and pray for one another.
Not because another human being replaces Christ.
Jesus alone paid the debt of sin.
But Christ never designed His people to fight every battle in isolation.
Maybe that is where this article found you.
Maybe your ministry hasn't been exposed.
Maybe your children still believe everything is okay.
Maybe your secret hasn't become a scandal.
And perhaps grace is reaching you before consequences have to scream what conviction has already been whispering.
Don't wait for devastation to become honest.
Don't wait until somebody catches you.
Don't wait until the doctor gives you frightening news.
Don't wait until your spouse finds the messages.
Don't wait until the debt becomes impossible.
Don't wait until the secret becomes public.
Don't wait until something you could have confronted in the light has consumed years in darkness.
There is no trophy for reaching rock bottom.
You are allowed to reach for Christ before everything collapses.
And if everything already has collapsed...
Because this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus is not merely Lord of the person you should have been.
He is Redeemer of the person standing in the wreckage.
The Corinthian church itself was filled with people whose former lives Paul could describe in painfully explicit terms.
Yet Scripture contains that astonishing phrase:
Your past can become past tense.
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write the ending.
Your secret does not sit on the throne.
Your craving does not sit on the throne.
Your shame does not sit on the throne.
Your addiction does not sit on the throne.
Your failure does not sit on the throne.
And perhaps repentance begins tonight without fireworks.
Maybe there is no dramatic music.
Maybe you're simply sitting alone with a phone in your hand and tears forming in your eyes.
And for once you stop saying...
That may be one of the most important sentences you ever pray.
“I want You more than I want this.”
And tomorrow the craving may still speak.
Repentance does not mean temptation instantly ceases to exist.
Recovery can involve setbacks, difficult days, accountability, rebuilding damaged trust, professional treatment, changed routines, boundaries, and repeated dependence upon God.
You stopped negotiating with the prison.
You stopped confusing secrecy with safety.
You finally called the thing what it was.
And you brought it toward the light.
That is why Paul's statement becomes more powerful when we continue reading the chapter.
He doesn't merely say, “Don't be mastered.”
He tells believers whose they are.
Your body belongs to the Lord.
You were bought with a price.
That is Christianity's answer to bondage.
You were purchased at immeasurable cost.
The hands stretched across the cross were pierced for sinners who could not rescue themselves.
The Savior who knew every filthy secret humanity would ever hide still walked toward Calvary.
He did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was deadly.
And He did not rise because redemption was impossible.
He rose because death itself could not keep the Son of God in the grave.
So when Jesus calls you out of darkness, He isn't trying to steal your pleasure.
He is calling you away from masters that cannot love you.
But they cannot bleed for you.
And maybe that's the sentence someone you know desperately needs tonight.
A reminder that there is a Savior stronger than the thing they are afraid to name.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't. We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
Someone you love may have spent years calling bondage a habit because “bondage” sounded too serious.
Maybe your share becomes the interruption.
Maybe your message becomes the doorway to confession.
And if this exposed something in you, don't disappear quietly.

Or, if Christ has already carried you through a season of bondage, leave a testimony that gives somebody else courage. You don't need to publish details that should remain private. Simply tell another wounded person that Jesus still redeems.
There may be a night when temptation becomes loud again and you need to remember the question:
“Am I choosing this—or has this begun choosing for me?”
Not because giving money earns salvation.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting the spread of biblical, Christ-centered content, one practical way you can participate is by supporting the work that produces and distributes it.
do the thing that matters infinitely more.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the promises you broke.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are terrified anyone else might see.
And then take whatever wise, concrete steps obedience requires to stop feeding what has been mastering you.
Because perhaps the scandal isn't simply that you became chained to something you once thought you controlled.
Perhaps the greater scandal is grace itself:
that Jesus already knew the ugliest chapter...
and still went to the cross.
And He still calls sinners out of darkness by name.
So stop giving your chains harmless names.
There is no shame in admitting that you need rescue when the One reaching toward you has scars in His hands.
The chain wants you to keep calling it a habit. Jesus is calling you into the light.
